parts.note: a bout fought with feather-filled cushions, the sort of romp children have just before going to bed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Featherweight' suggests a boxing division and 'retirement' a boxer quitting, but the feathers are in the weapons and retiring means going to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedtime battle with stuffed cushions is literally a contest of feathers that precedes sleep.

clue.text: Accustom' to being, at home on river

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: in means at home
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: Getting used to living at home beside a river.
explanation.definitionFit: To harden someone to hardship is to make them used to it.

clue.text: Cutlet served with top of endive or other salad

indicators.note: the cutlet is served up, so its letters are dished out in a new order
the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter

explanation.surface: A chop comes with endive or some other leafy side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Served' rearranges CUTLET into LETTUC; 'top of' adds E, endive's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lettuce is a leafy green that, like endive, forms the base of a salad.

parts.note: a mural is painted on a wall, so wall stands for it
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A painting on a wall takes a heavy blow.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a heavy thump is to strike forcefully.

clue.text: Jokingly, we hear, boy swallowed food

indicators.note: the words are heard spoken, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

parts.note: jokingly is 'in jest'
Ed is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A boy, said to be kidding, ate up his meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We hear' applies to 'Jokingly' alone: 'in jest' said out loud gives INGEST, then the boy ED is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking food into the body by mouth is ingestion.

parts.note: the prefix used when the Spanish form part of a compound word, as in a term joining Spain with another nation

explanation.walkthrough: 'Combinations' are compound words, not underwear or safe locks.
explanation.definitionFit: The combining form for Spain appears in compound adjectives, so it describes the Spanish within such words.

indicators.note: out means wrong or disordered, so the letters are put in another order

explanation.surface: The police issue a notice to discard a repeating gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Met' looks like the London police but stands for the Meteorological Office, Britain's weather service.
explanation.definitionFit: A Met Office bulletin is a forecast of rain, sun and wind.

indicators.note: the word for swiftly follows, coming after the vehicle

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
apace means swiftly

explanation.surface: A rigid-roofed car comes speeding along behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard-top' is a car with a fixed roof, but here it is a shell, as on a tortoise or crab.
explanation.definitionFit: The rigid upper shell of a turtle or crab is a hard covering on its top.

explanation.surface: Someone tumbles down a spiral in a chaotic rush.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairground spiral slide winds down like a screw thread; as an adverb it means in confused hurry.

indicators.note: the answer is made of letters taken from inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone escapes from a jail in the uptown part of a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooler' is slang for prison, which makes the surface a jailbreak; the letters sit across the join of 'cooler' and 'uptown'.
explanation.definitionFit: A volcano or a riot bursts forth suddenly, which is to break out.

clue.text: Member is not on time to make legal provisions

parts.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body
someone not on time is late

explanation.surface: A Member of Parliament who is late gets round to passing laws.
explanation.definitionFit: Passing statutes is what lawmakers do; to frame such provisions is to enact laws.

indicators.note: a housing development rebuilds the slum, and here the letters of the two words are rebuilt

explanation.surface: Residents are nervous about building work on a run-down estate at the edge of town.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fearful trembles, quivering with nerves.

parts.note: vast means very great in size

explanation.surface: A tremendous halt called out to a ship's crew.
explanation.definitionFit: An old nautical command telling sailors to cease what they are doing.

clue.text: Hole-in a shoe doesn't cause it to leak

definitions.text: Hole-in a shoe doesn't cause it to leak

parts.words: Hole-in a shoe doesn't cause it to leak
parts.note: a hole in footwear that lets in no water: the small reinforced ring through which the lace is threaded

explanation.walkthrough: A hole in a shoe normally lets water in; this one is made deliberately to take the lace.
explanation.definitionFit: A small metal-rimmed opening for a lace is a deliberate perforation that keeps the shoe sound.

parts.note: expo is short for exposition, a large exhibition
sure means certain

explanation.surface: A trade fair is guaranteed to get media coverage.
explanation.definitionFit: Coverage in the media gives something attention and public visibility.

parts.note: a debutante, or deb, is a young woman 'coming out' into society
someone elated is 'walking on air', so on air

explanation.surface: A delightful young woman makes her society debut in high spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming out' is the old phrase for a young woman's first formal entry into high society, which makes her a debutante.
explanation.definitionFit: A debonair person is suave and pleasantly charming in manner.

clue.text: Sea, caught in marsh-grass, did not ebb

indicators.note: one word is trapped inside the other, as if snagged among the stems

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass of marshes
the main is an old word for the open sea

explanation.surface: Seawater trapped among the rushes stayed put instead of draining away.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that did not ebb stayed where it was, continued without falling back.

clue.text: Peter Orr trained as a correspondent

indicators.note: when the man's name is trained, its letters are drilled into a new order

explanation.surface: A man named Peter Orr was schooled for a career writing for the newspapers.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper correspondent is a journalist who files stories from a place.

indicators.note: not quite the whole thing, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: true is real and blue is Tory, the colour of Britain's Conservatives

explanation.surface: A US estate agent is almost a staunch Conservative.
explanation.walkthrough: True-blue is British slang for a staunch Conservative; split it as true (REAL) plus blue (TORY), then 'Not quite' drops the final Y.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US an estate agent who sells houses and land is called by this term.

clue.text: Make quick run, leaving cover behind?

definitions.text: Make quick run, leaving cover behind?

parts.words: Make quick run, leaving cover behind?
parts.note: a dash done with one's clothes left behind, a naked sprint across a public place

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaving cover behind' sounds like a soldier breaking cover, but the cover is clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To dash naked through a public place is to run without clothes, which is exactly the slang verb's sense.

clue.text: Could be a charter right away for internal airline.

indicators.note: the words could be rearranged into something else, so their letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A chartered flight might serve as an internal air route if right away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right away' takes R out of A CHARTER; 'Could be' rearranges the rest. 'Airline' is an air passage in the body, not a carrier.
explanation.definitionFit: The windpipe carries air through the body's interior, a pipeline for breath.

explanation.surface: Small pieces from a series of brawls.
explanation.definitionFit: Leftover fragments are odds and ends; brawls or squabbles are also called by this word.

parts.note: Pa is Dad, so Pa's
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: Asking what the Home Guard of the old TV comedy ate.
explanation.walkthrough: Dad's Army is a British TV sitcom about the wartime Home Guard; here it splits into Pa's TA.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaghetti and macaroni are wheat-based dishes rich in carbohydrate.

explanation.surface: Asking about the main liquor served in a Russian harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: A chief angel such as Gabriel is a principal heavenly spirit; it is also the English name of the White Sea port Arkhangelsk.

clue.text: Ends of greybeard enfolding our skin

indicators.note: enfolding means wrapping around, so one piece goes round the other
the ends of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: An old man's beard wraps around our faces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ends of' gives G and D, the first and last letters of 'greybeard', which go round OUR.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard dried rind of a calabash fruit is used as a vessel, a shell or skin.

parts.note: the imaginary kingdom invented by the novelist Anthony Hope in The Prisoner of Zenda

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase recalls 'Land of Hope and Glory', the patriotic British song, but Hope is the author.
explanation.definitionFit: The novelist Anthony Hope set his Zenda romances in this made-up central European kingdom.

clue.text: Hospital love to employ everybody in theatre

parts.note: H is the map and sign abbreviation for hospital
love is nil in tennis, the letter O
to employ is to use

explanation.surface: A hospital loves to put on shows for the whole audience.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole audience in a theatre is called the house, as in 'a full house'.

clue.text: At some matches, they hold up trains

definitions.text: At some matches, they hold up trains

parts.words: At some matches, they hold up trains
parts.note: at weddings, attendants carry the long trailing back of the bride's dress

explanation.walkthrough: 'Matches' are weddings, not games, and 'hold up trains' means carrying a dress, not robbing a railway.
explanation.definitionFit: Bridal attendants lift the long trailing hem of the wedding gown as the bride walks.
